https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.title: Swampy and Tory peer join forces against Just Stop Oil’s radical climate protests
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/environment/.text:
A Tory peer and Swampy are joining forces to establish a new climate group that rejects the radical protest methods used by Just Stop Oil and Extinction Rebellion.
The Climate Majority Project (CMP), which launches next week, counts among its backers Lord Randall of Uxbridge, former environment adviser to Theresa May, as well as Dale Vince, the green energy industrialist and Labour donor. Dan Hooper, better known as “Swampy”, is also involved, as are former leaders of Extinction Rebellion (XR), including Rupert Read, who is co-director of the new group.
CMP was formed in response to the methods employed by groups such as Just Stop Oil, whose members have blockaded roads and disrupted fuel supplies. According to its manifesto, the new group pitches itself as a moderate alternative to those that have come before by undertaking “climate action that [is] accessible and persuasive to a majority of people”.
In a statement sent to The Times announcing the project, the group says: “Afraid of sounding alarmist, millions stay silent. So the majority and its power are hidden. It’s time for the climate majority to make its voice heard.” Among 24 people backing the statement are Chris Packham, the BBC broadcaster, and Sir Geoff Mulgan, former director or policy at Downing Street under Tony Blair.
Swampy rose to national prominence in 1996 after he spent a week in a tunnel protesting against the expansion of the A30 in Devon. He has been involved with XR activism and in 2021 helped with the construction and occupation of tunnels at Euston Square Gardens in London in opposition to HS2.
Asked on Monday about collaborating with the tunneler, Randall, who is one of those backing the statement, said: “I’m not a fan of direct action at all, and while this may make me unpopular with some of my co-signatories, I think it has the reverse effect, in that it puts people off. Everyone has a different way of showing their opposition, and while I would be happy to have a chat with Swampy about his views, it doesn’t necessarily mean I’m going to jump into a hole with him.”

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.title: I was violated by a police spy — and the state gave its blessing
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.subtitle: As a report prepares to set out how undercover officers slept with their targets, one victim tells her story for the first time
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/law/article/.text:
Eleanor Fairbraida was harvesting salad on an organic farm in the Yorkshire Dales when she received the phone call that would turn her world on its head.
The close friend she had known as Mark Stone, a seemingly committed environmental activist with whom she had been intimate over a number of months, was in fact an undercover police officer, she was told.
His real name was Mark Kennedy, and for the past seven years he had been working for Scotland Yard to spy on Fairbraida and dozens of other climate change protesters across Europe.
As part of the deception — one of the biggest policing scandals in modern times — Kennedy slept with at least ten women between 2003 and 2010. He also hid the fact that he was married and had two children.
“It was a huge betrayal of trust,” Fairbraida recalled this weekend. “It was a horrific violation, it was non-consensual and it was supported by the state.”
Her decision to speak out publicly for the first time coincides with the revelation that Kennedy, a former officer in the secretive National Public Order Intelligence Unit (NPOIU), is being investigated over allegations of criminal misconduct.
Detectives recently interviewed Fairbraida, 45, as a witness and are seeking evidence from other alleged victims about Kennedy’s sexual activities and claims he may have acted as an agent provocateur to incite criminality.
Kennedy, 53, is one of at least 130 undercover officers employed by the NPOIU and its predecessor unit, the Special Demonstration Squad, whose spying activities are being examined by a separate public inquiry.
They operated in secret for more than 50 years and monitored more than 1,000 political groups, including anti-apartheid campaigners, and even the family of Stephen Lawrence, the black teenager murdered by racist thugs in 1993.
“It’s something that you’d think would happen in East Germany or China,” Fairbraida said.
Many of the officers were issued with fake identities taken from dead babies. Some fathered children with the women they had been tasked to spy on.
The undercover policing inquiry, led by Sir John Mitting, a former High Court judge, is due to publish its first report at the end of this month.
Fairbraida, who has sons aged five and eight, and three grown-up stepchildren from her husband’s previous relationship, has waived her right to anonymity to speak about her own experience. Until last week, she was listed as a core participant of the Mitting inquiry under the alias “Jane”.
The daughter of distinguished archaeologists, Fairbraida was raised in rural Hampshire and studied biology at New College, Oxford. “I grew up in the countryside and I’ve always been very passionate about nature,” she said.
By 2003, she had moved to Nottingham, where she became involved with Earth First!, a direct-action group operating out of the volunteer-run Sumac Centre in the city.
The centre was a hub for left-wing and radical groups involved in civil disobedience and appears to have been picked by Kennedy and his handlers as a starting point for his infiltration operation.
Fairbraida believes she was the first activist he met. “He said he’d had a nasty break-up with a girlfriend in London and that he needed to start a new life,” she recalled.
“He had long hair, piercings and tattoos — he kind-of looked the part,” she said. “He certainly didn’t look like a policeman.”
Kennedy — or Stone as she knew him then — said he was keen to attend a national gathering of regional Earth First! groups that summer in Yorkshire. Their friendship began after he agreed to give Fairbraida a lift to the event in his van.
“Not many people had their own vehicles, so it was like an asset,” she said. “Not only did he have a van, but he was up for using it, driving around to demos and gatherings. He made himself available and enthusiastically took part.”
Kennedy also seemed to have a lot more money than Fairbraida and his new activist friends, earning him the nickname “Flash”. He claimed the money came from doing delivery work for his “Uncle Phil” in London. Fairbraida believes, in hindsight, that this was probably a reference to his Scotland Yard handler.
Towards the end of 2003, Kennedy moved in to a house in Nottingham with Fairbraida and two other activists — the first of three properties they would share together.
Soon afterwards, he started a sexual relationship with Kate Wilson, one of Fairbraida’s friends from Oxford and the only other British woman abused by Kennedy to disclose her real identity.
Nobody suspected a thing and, over time, Kennedy reportedly travelled to 22 countries to take part in — and monitor — a wave of climate change and anticapitalist protests.
They included the G8 summit at Gleneagles in Scotland in 2005 and violent actions on the Continent organised by ”black bloc” anarchists.
“Kennedy put himself out as someone who really hated the police,” Fairbraida said. “He was involved in burning things. He was a really trusted and central activist.”
He perfected the act by learning to play the guitar, becoming a drum-and-bass DJ and even indulging in performance poetry.
By the autumn of 2008, Fairbraida was single and found herself flirting with Kennedy after several years as close friends. He had split up with Wilson but had started another relationship with a Welsh-born activist known as “Lisa”.
“He invited me on a date to see an awful rock band at the Old Angel [pub in Nottingham]” said Fairbraida. “We got very drunk and we slept together.”
Although there was no emotional connection between them, Fairbraida said they carried on having sex for about six months. Lisa was aware of the fling, she said, because their circle of friends believed in polyamory.
It was Kennedy’s six-year relationship with Lisa that eventually led to his double life unravelling.
The couple were on a campervan holiday in Italy in July 2010 when Lisa discovered a passport in the glove box bearing the name Mark Kennedy. She also found an old mobile phone that contained messages from two children referring to their “dad”, according to The Guardian.
Lisa raised her concerns with other activist friends, who later obtained a birth certificate for one of Kennedy’s children. It listed the father’s occupation as “police officer”.
In October 2010, six activists confronted Kennedy directly with the evidence, prompting a tearful confession.
The activists then set about alerting all the women they knew Kennedy had slept with, including Fairbraida, who by that stage was living in a caravan on a farm in the Yorkshire Dales.
Fairbraida said the revelation that her former housemate had been an undercover police officer was “a complete mindf***”. This was a man, she said, she had trusted with her life on countless protests. “I loved him as a friend, dearly,” she added.
Her main concern at the time, however, was Lisa. “She was completely broken,” Fairbraida said, holding back tears. “He’s had six years of her prime life when she could have been having children. He was everything to her — and it was just a lie.”
Fairbraida initially considered herself simply “unlucky” for ending up in a sexual relationship with Kennedy. At one point she even blamed herself: “I felt castigated and shamed that I’d been infiltrated in this way. I felt ‘I must have done something really wrong’.”
Her friend Wilson, 42, later won damages and an apology from the Metropolitan Police as part of a group action. Wilson also launched a case — supported by Fairbraida — at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal.
In September 2021, the tribunal ruled that Wilson’s human rights had been breached and that Kennedy had “grossly debased, degraded and humiliated” her by deceiving her into a relationship.
The tribunal judgment added that senior officers supervising Kennedy “either knew of the relationship, chose not to know of its existence, or were incompetent and negligent in not following up on the clear and obvious signs”.
Fairbraida’s involvement as a witness in the case meant she was given access to police logs that had been compiled about her. They contained the bombshell that she had been a specific “target” of Kennedy’s spying operation. Fairbraida is now convinced that he deliberately slept with her to win her trust.
She believes Kennedy also tried to set her up with another undercover officer, called “Vinny”, whom he claimed was a friend from London.
“There has been this unit [the NPOIU] that’s been enabling male police officers to go out and behave in a predatory manner towards young women,” Fairbraida said.
Following his unmasking more than a decade ago, Kennedy hired Max Clifford as his publicist and sold his story to a national newspaper.
He later blamed the Met for failing to “protect” him from falling in love with the environmental campaigners he had been sent to infiltrate.
After resigning from the force, he briefly continued his undercover work, pretending to be an animal rights activist for a private investigations company supplying intelligence to big corporations.
Kennedy is now believed to be at the centre of a criminal investigation into misconduct in public office. Codenamed Operation Montrose, it is being led by Detective Chief Inspector Kirstie Masters, a Met officer seconded to the National Police Chiefs’ Council (NPCC). The NPCC said no arrests have been made. “As this is an ongoing investigation, we cannot provide any further comment,” a spokesman said. Kennedy declined to comment.
Like Fairbraida, Kennedy has also been given core participant status in the Mitting inquiry.
Launched in 2015 by Theresa May, the home secretary at the time, the inquiry — which has already cost more than £64 million — is divided into six tranches. A report into the first tranche, covering the activities of police spies from 1968 to 1982, will be published on June 29.
Public hearings dealing with Kennedy and the NPOIU are unlikely to commence until 2025.
“Kennedy destroyed lives, but the problem goes far beyond him, right up the ranks,” said Elizabeth Forrester, a solicitor at Birnberg Peirce, who represents Fairbraida. “We want the inquiry to hold his superior officers to account. We want to hear them give evidence and to ask them questions.”
Fairbraida, who now lives in Bristol and does charity work, attends only the occasional public demonstration these days, including one in London in April led by Extinction Rebellion.
Her experience with Kennedy has left her struggling to trust others, particularly in the sphere of political organising, and she eschews the direct-action stunts that got her repeatedly arrested in her youth.
“I see what I’m doing now as activism,” Fairbraida said. “I have a platform because I had a sexual relationship with Kennedy. But for me, the bigger story is about the corruption of our democracy.”
She admits that speaking out under her real name “feels scary”. “But it also feels empowering. I’m not hiding. I’m saying, ‘Actually, I’m not ashamed of what I was doing’.
“In fact, I’m proud of what I was doing and I shouldn’t have been infiltrated.”

https://www.thetimes.com/article/dale-vi.title: Dale Vince: ‘I admire Just Stop Oil, they’re trying to wake this country up’
https://www.thetimes.com/article/dale-vi.text:
Dale Vince is Britain’s most successful hippy. Forty years ago, having dropped out of school at 15, he was living off grid in a converted ambulance, too poor to afford shoes, eating leftovers from rubbish bins.
Then the lorry driver’s son from Norfolk made himself a wind turbine to stick on his roof and decided “to get into the big stuff”. Now the UK’s first green energy company, Ecotricity, which he founded in 1995, is worth £100 million. But he would never call himself super-rich, instead saying: “I’m well-off.”
He’s just moved into a barge near Tewkesbury close to his offices in Stroud, where he once squatted, and while he is chairman of a football club, Forest Green Rovers, it’s carbon neutral and vegan like its owner. “I don’t have credit cards or a mortgage, a second home or exotic holidays,” he says. “I just need my rucksack and electric motorbike.”
Yet this 61-year-old, who still dresses in old T-shirts and wears a shark’s tooth necklace, has become the most contentious environmental millionaire in Britain, after it emerged he is helping to fund both the campaigning group Just Stop Oil and the Labour Party.
Just Stop Oil protesters have thrown soup at a masterpiece, disrupted the snooker, caused havoc at cricket matches, despoiled the Chelsea Flower Show and ruined thousands of people’s daily lives by blocking roads. Their tactics have been dismissed as frivolous and futile — Vince may not be making himself popular by helping their cause.
But the author of the bestselling new book Manifesto: the Battle for Green Britain doesn’t feel guilty. “For 13 years we’ve had a series of dysfunctional Tory regimes, more focused on saving themselves than the country,” he says. “Of course, I can see why Just Stop Oil are frustrated, they want everyone to focus on the climate catastrophe, not petty political manoeuvring.”
Vince, who looks as though he has just wandered in from the beach, rather than his office, appears laid-back but is adamant. “I admire Just Stop Oil, they’re prepared to risk their freedom to stop the government opening yet more new coal mines and taking more resources out of the North Sea on the false premise it will bring down energy prices when all it has done is create windfall profits for the companies.”
This week, the reluctant millionaire even said he would double donations offered to the protest group for the next 24 hours. “That was my flicking two fingers at all those media outlets stirring stories about me,” he says, laughing.
Is it fair to ruin sporting and arts events for fans, particularly when so many people are struggling post-pandemic and through a cost-of-living crisis to find some respite? “Is it fair that last summer 40,000 people lost their lives in Europe due to excess extreme heat, or that half of Pakistan was flooded and people lost their homes? Just Stop Oil are disrupting business as usual because they are trying to wake this country up to far greater potential devastation.”
However, it’s the poor cleaners who have to mop up when they throw soup or paint. “I don’t agree with damaging art or property, it’s a form of aggression and from a campaigning point it’s a mistake,” Vince says. “But I’m just saying I understand their strong feelings. I find it ironic that we can tolerate this climate crisis but not a bit of disruption to snooker. This is going to be the most damaging event that we as a species have ever experienced.”
The protests have antagonised many who might have been supporters. “I don’t know if it’s counterproductive but what they are creating is headlines and a platform. There’s no point in just waving placards and chanting slogans, people won’t listen.”
But Vince won’t criticise the police either. “They may be dragging people off the roads but they have a job to do upholding the law. It’s the government who are behaving in a draconian way, their crackdown on protesters feels as authoritarian as Russia now.”
However, even Sir Keir Starmer, whom he supports, has called them wrong and arrogant. “No party can advocate law-breaking,” Vince replies. The businessman has given over £1.5 million to the Labour Party coffers in recent years. Did he influence the Labour leader’s decision last week to announce plans to ban new North Sea oil and gas development if the party wins the next general election?
“I think I have spoken to Keir twice briefly on the phone, once was last week. He just thanked me for my support. I’ve never met him, but I like the direction of Labour under his leadership. He’s impressive, a man of huge integrity and purpose. Labour gets the green agenda, they can see the economic opportunities. The move to green energy isn’t just about the climate, it’s about creating jobs and strengthening our economy.”
Yet, having been a communist as a teenager, a part of Vince must recoil at big business donating to parties? “I would prefer us to publicly fund parties, but one of the reasons I give money is to help fund the gap between the Tories and every other party on funding. They have big money from greedy fossil fuel companies, housebuilders and the City.”
Vince believes the next general election will be the most important for a generation. “We will be halfway through the last decade the UN said we had to avoid the worst of the temperature rises, and as Boris Johnson would say, so far we have spaffed that time up the wall.”
Green issues, he insists, can be populist if Labour make it clear they will improve people’s lives financially. “A lot of people are struggling with bills, this could be a win-win; 100 per cent homegrown energy from our renewables will make us less dependent on shock energy rises. This isn’t just about polar bears, it’s about bringing down the cost of living.”
When he created some of the first wind turbines in the 1990s, Vince was dismissed as a crank. “Yet now we are at 50 per cent green electricity on the grid. We have come a long way, the technology has matured and is now the cheapest.”
Once again, he is being ridiculed for believing that Britain can now be self-reliant on renewable energy. “There is enough onshore wind to power the country four times over, enough onshore solar to power the country eight times over, and if we throw in a bit of offshore wind power, we can get to 20 times over,” he says.
“We will only need one per cent of Britain’s land to be 100 per cent self-sufficient. Wind and solar are so fast to build that we can do them in 12 months. In every way they are superior to extracting more resources from the North Sea.”
Vince is also evangelical about electric cars, having built the first prototype in Britain years ago. “The big manufacturers have now piled in and that’s good, because the cost of buying them has come down, but the government needs to take VAT off electric cars and make them easier to own. It’s no good being stuck on the motorway without a charging point.”
His fellow multimillionaires prefer private jets. “I wouldn’t ban them, but I would tax them very highly and put fuel duty on aviation. You’re encouraged to fly with cheap tickets and duty-free shopping, but we don’t we have that on greener trains or buses. It’s absurd.” In France, the government has cracked down on internal flights. “That’s not going to happen with this prime minister. Rishi Sunak likes to jump in a plane or chopper to get around the country.”
Vince won’t fly until he finds a greener solution. “I haven’t flown for a long time, I’m not sure I ever have holidays. I like Cornwall, I went to Paris by train last week. Flying looks like the last frontier, something we have to give up, but the technology is coming, we are launching an electric airline soon and then maybe we can fly completely carbon-free planes across Europe.”
Space, however, is a frontier too far. “Space tourism is just an ego trip for self-obsessed billionaires.” He is known for his dislike of Elon Musk, after they fell out over creating infrastructure for electric cars. “Space tourism is the pinnacle of what is bad about polluting humans and our obsession with the super-rich. It makes Jeff Bezos and Musk look ridiculous.”
Vince may be greener than thou, but he faces an uphill battle to convince others to join him in his carbon-neutral, vegan-fest. After a rush on Greggs vegan sausage rolls, the market for vegetable-based food has collapsed as people struggle with their grocery bills.
“In the last 30 years there has been a 30 per cent reduction in red meat but recently there has been a vegan bubble, lots of greedy people piled in and it was over-saturated. Plant-based foods should be cheaper, more delicious and nutritious. Our football club went vegan ten years ago and no one complains.”
The Forest Green chairman says he would rather die than eat meat. “I’ve been vegan 40 years and don’t take any supplements. I wouldn’t eat pig to save my life. I’d prefer to starve.” He sounds too virtuous to be true. “I’m not sure if I have many Achilles’ heels in my lifestyle. My biggest vice is probably chips, I drink a bit and I like to party.”
He doesn’t want to call people out; when I met him once on a radio show he didn’t raise an eyebrow as the rest of the panel ate pepperoni pizzas. “Just do what you can.” But he makes an exception for the prime minister. “Rishi Sunak’s heated swimming pool makes him out of touch as a billionaire. What kind of message are you sending when, in the middle of an energy and cost of living crisis, you build a vast pool and have to upgrade the grid to heat it? I am wealthy but I do remember being homeless.”
Unlike most of us who might appreciate £100 million, Vince still sounds uncomfortable about his money. “I don’t feel rich, it’s a paper fortune, I don’t even have a savings account. I have no pensions or second property. But I don’t have the worries either. I have an electric Harley-Davidson, that’s my extravagance.”
He could have stood as Labour MP for Stroud if he wanted to extend his influence. “I think I am more of an inventor and disruptor, I like making things happen. All the things we did as the first green energy company are finally being picked up now.”
One day he wants to return to the road in his campervan. “I’ve just converted an old Volkswagen to electric, I feel sometimes too busy and I don’t have enough time to live. But there hasn’t been a more important time to get out there and be a catalyst for green change and renewables.”
For the moment, now his three children are grown up, he’s comfortable living in his Dutch barge. “I’m making it solar powered and I’m changing the diesel engine. I see swans, ducks and rabbits every morning where I am moored. It’s super peaceful. I have a tiny airfry oven for my vegan burgers. I eat salad, beetroot and garlic and make my own hummus. I’d like to grow my own vegetables, but my mind is too busy and impatient. Life is a building project. I always want to improve stuff whether at home or for the country.”
Born: August 29, 1961
Education: Left school at 15. Given honorary degree of doctor of philosophy by the University of Gloucestershire.
Career: Founded the Renewable Energy Company, now known as Ecotricity, in 1995 and launched his first wind turbine in 1996. Given an OBE in 2004 for services to the environment and to the electricity industry.
In 2010 became a major shareholder of Forest Green Rovers FC, and was later appointed club chairman. Has donated to the Labour Party and the Green Party, endorsing the Green Party’s Caroline Lucas at the 2015 UK general election.
Endorsed the Labour Party in the 2019 general election and has donated roughly £1.5 million to the party in the past decade. In April 2022, he decided to sell Ecotricity. Has donated to environmental protest groups, such as Just Stop Oil, Extinction Rebellion, Greenpeace and Sea Shepherd Conservation Society.
Family: He has three children.
Greggs vegan sausage roll or organic bacon buttie? Vegan every time
Game of Thrones or Succession? Game of Thrones
Jerusalem or Enron? Jerusalem, the play and the poem
House or campervan? Campervan
Swimming pool or pond? The sea, ponds are a bit muddy
Pedal bike or motorbike? Electric motorbike
Champagne or chips? Chips
Manifesto: How a Maverick Entrepreneur Took On British Energy and Won by Dale Vince is published by Ebury Press

image.caption: Dale Vince has been vegan for 40 years and said he would rather starve than eat meatADRIAN SHERRATT FOR THE TIMES

https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.title: Just Stop Oil: police use new powers to arrest protesters in London
https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.subtitle: Law changed to redefine ‘serious disruption’
https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.text:
Just Stop Oil protesters used air horns and glitter cannon to disrupt a performance of Dialogues des Carmélites at Glyndebourne yesterday, even though the festival has its own wind turbine.
Three people were escorted out of the front row after they brought the opera festival, near Lewes in East Sussex, to a halt at about 5.30pm.
Boos and cries of “get out” can be heard in footage from the incident. An audience member said: “The confetti cannon sounded like gunshot. Many people screamed. I don’t think they’ve won this lot over to their cause.”
Stephen Langridge, Glyndebourne’s artistic director, took to the stage to ask the audience to remain patient. He said the conductor, Robin Ticciati, needed time to compose himself before getting back in the pit after the loud bang went off right next to his ear.
Golda Schultz, the South African soprano performing the part of Madame Lidoine, tweeted: “We soldier on! Wish they had done their research before doing that. This festival and house is one of the greenest places I’ve ever worked. So many could learn from their sustainable and carbon neutralising practices!” The protesters said the action was taken to demand that the government halt all licences for new oil, gas and coal projects.
Glyndebourne installed a 67-metre turbine in 2012, against local opposition. It now provides more than 90 per cent of the company’s annual electricity needs and has helped deliver an 83 per reduction in its energy-related emissions since 2009. A spokeswoman for Glyndebourne apologised to everyone whose visit was affected by the protest. “At approximately 5.31pm, today’s performance of Poulenc’s Dialogues des Carmélites was disrupted by three protesters who let off a confetti bomb, blew an air horn and started shouting,” she said. “The stage was immediately cleared and within less than a minute ushers had peacefully escorted the protesters from the theatre. The audience remained inside the theatre and were provided with regular updates and, following a 21-minute delay, the opera restarted at approximately 5.52pm.
“We have formally reported the incident to the police but the police were not on site and no arrests were made.”
Earlier, more than a dozen Just Stop Oil protesters were arrested on slow marches through London, on the same day police were given new powers to intervene more quickly to prevent disruption. Fifty-four activists began marching on the A406 at Hanger Lane, west London and at Battersea Bridge, south London, at 8am, continuing daily protests that have run for six weeks.
Police were handed the new powers after a law change cleared its final hurdle in the House of Lords this week. This gives a wider definition of “serious disruption” under the Public Order Act 1986, including tackling delay, hindrance or disruption that is “more than minor”.

image.caption: Police remove a Just Stop Oil protester at Vauxhall, London, on the day they were handed new powers to halt disruptionGUY BELL/ALAMY

https://www.thetimes.com/article/chris-p.title: Chris Packham film asks if more climate protesters must break the law
https://www.thetimes.com/article/chris-p.text:
Chris Packham has called for a “tornado of change” to tackle the climate crisis and questioned whether peaceful protest is making enough of a difference.
The naturalist and presenter, a regular donor to the Just Stop Oil campaign, is preparing to front a Channel 4 documentary provisionally entitled Is It Time to Break the Law?.
In the film, to be aired this summer, Packham will assess the impact of protests by those who have broken the law and been imprisoned and ask whether more people should risk arrest.
“Peaceful protest has been a cornerstone of activism, but as the urgency grows, we must question whether it is enough,” Packham said.
“What will compel decision-makers to listen and take decisive action? The time for complacency has long passed, and it is up to us to drive a tornado of change that cannot be ignored. Our planet’s survival depends on it.”
He added that policymakers had consistently failed to make headway. “Scientists, activists and naturalists like myself have been delving deep into the pressing issues surrounding the climate crisis for decades, shedding light on the disheartening reality that governments continue to fall short on their environmental promises.”
• Laws ‘rushed through’ to stop slow-walking protests
The film will explore the view of activists who believe the situation has become so dire that they must follow the example of the suffragettes, who damaged property and chained themselves to railings to improve women’s rights, and Mahatma Gandhi, who was repeatedly imprisoned for defying British laws.
Last month Packham, 62, said he considered the 2½-year prison sentences handed to two Just Stop Oil protesters for climbing the Dartford Crossing bridge to be “disproportionate”.
He added that the “very dangerous path” Britain had taken with its protest laws had led him to wonder how an autistic person like him would cope with prison.
“Would I be functional in jail? The answer is very probably, definitely, no. So do I therefore avoid going to jail to have greater influence outside? Probably the answer is yes,” he said.
The documentary’s producer, David DeHaney, said: “This journey of standing up to injustice while forging a positive blueprint for change is one that we often feature in our programmes, but never before has it felt so urgent, or universally resonant.”
Is It Time to Break the Law? will be screened as part of a climate change season on Channel 4. In Beef vs Chicken: The Big Switch, the presenter Ade Adepitan will cast doubt on the environmental benefits of veganism. He will meet campaigners attempting to “make beef the new smoking” as he examines the claim that substituting white meat for red is a comparatively small change that would bring a big reduction in greenhouse gas emissions.

image.caption: Chris Packham has been a supporter of the Just Stop Oil campaignTIMES PHOTOGRAPHER JACK HILL

https://www.thetimes.com/article/labour-.title: Labour threw me under a bus, says spurned donor Ian Rosenblatt
https://www.thetimes.com/article/labour-.text:
A senior City lawyer has accused the Labour Party of throwing him under the bus and warned other business people to be wary of donating after the party said it was returning his donations.
Ian Rosenblatt, a lifelong Labour supporter who backed Sir Keir Starmer’s leadership campaign, had pledged to donate £150,000 to Labour over three years after the election of Starmer. He donated almost £200,000 to the Labour Party when Ed Miliband was leader.
Labour returned his most recent £16,000 donation yesterday, hours after a newspaper raised questions about work that Rosenblatt, the law firm named after him, had carried out for the sanctioned Russian bank VTB Capital.
The law firm was appointed by VTB in October, largely to carry out work for the UK-based restructuring firm Teneo, which was appointed as administrator of VTB UK. The work was carried out under a licence from the Office of Financial Sanctions Implementation, a Treasury body. The firm did not work for VTB Capital before the bank was sanctioned by ministers.
Rosenblatt is no longer an employee, nor is he a director of the law firm, which is owned by the Aim-listed RBG Holdings, although he still retains a significant stake. He was not part of the legal team that dealt with the case involving VTB Capital.
“To say I have profited from Russia is ridiculous,” he said. “I don’t know every bit of work going on in a law firm that employs 250 people; I’m not involved in the day-to-day management.”
Rosenblatt had a brief conversation with the Labour peer Lord Alli, the party’s chief fundraiser. “There was no due process,” he said. “It was a unilateral decision. The whole thing happened in about an hour. It only became a story when the Labour Party said it would return the money. It sounds like I am guilty of doing something wrong.”
He warned other business leaders and investors to be wary of donating to the Labour Party. “If you are a Labour-inclined executive, investor or businessman be careful,” he said. “If they don’t like the colour of the socks they will throw you under the bus.”
Labour has in recent weeks come under fire for accepting more than £1.5 million from Dale Vince, the multimillionaire founder of the green energy firm Ecotricity. Vince has been a high-profile supporter of the radical environmental group Just Stop Oil.
The Labour Party has been approached for a comment.

image.caption: Ian Rosenblatt had a £16,000 donation to the party returned after questions were raised about work that his law firm had carried out for a sanctioned Russian bankJC OLIVERA / GETTY IMAGES / WIREIMAGE

https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.title: Just Stop Oil fundraiser tells activists: Just stop — it’s not helping
https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.text:
Trevor Neilson emanates a surprising breeziness for a man who is about to disown a prominent part of his life’s work, chastise friends and former colleagues, and call into question the movement he helped start.
Neilson, 50, is a wealthy California entrepreneur, and looks the part. On a sunny day last week at the office of his start-up in the wealthy Pacific Palisades area, a stone’s throw from the crashing surf, Neilson sports a T-shirt, jeans, slip-on shoes, and the air of a man ready to unburden himself.
Four years ago, Neilson tapped his network of billionaires and Hollywood A-listers to bankroll what he called a “wild-ass idea”: to finance a band of extremist activists, mostly in London and Europe, who would use guerrilla tactics to wake up the world to the climate emergency.
The organisation he started, the Climate Emergency Fund (CEF), gave birth to and became the prime financial backer of Extinction Rebellion and Just Stop Oil, among more than 100 other activist groups, which have become infamous for lying in the streets and “slow marching” through London, causing traffic snarl-ups. They have thrown soup on Van Gogh’s Sunflowers in the National Gallery, defaced buildings, glued themselves to walls and disrupted football matches.
From his home in Malibu, Neilson, once an enthusiastic supporter of such tactics, has watched with growing unease. And now he has chosen to speak out, for the first time, about what has gone wrong with the movement he helped launch.
The protesters, he said, have lost the plot, veering from clear-eyed radicals catalysing change to unserious rabble-rousers who are actually holding back the cause. “It’s become disruption for the sake of disruption. Working people that are trying to get to their job, get their kid dropped off at school, survive a brutal cost of living crisis in the UK, you know, there’s a certain hierarchy of needs that they have. If at the same time they have a pink-haired, tattooed and pierced protester standing in front of their car, so that their kid is late for their test that day, that does not encourage them to join the movement,” he said. “It’s just performative. It’s not accomplishing anything. I absolutely believe that it has now become counterproductive, and I just feel like that has to be said by somebody that was involved in the beginnings of what it has become.”
Indeed, it emerged last week that Just Stop Oil, which has reportedly received more than £1 million from the CEF — the fund declined to give specific numbers— plans to disrupt Wimbledon. The British public has become increasingly exasperated with their tactics. A group of protesters “slow marching” through Camden, north London, on Thursday had a bucket of water thrown over them from a block of flats and a passer-by screamed: “I’ve got to get to work and get my kids. Now I’m late! Do you think this is acceptable?!”
Neilson’s argument is that the time for such tactics has passed. When he co-founded the CEF in 2019, he recalled, “No one was talking about climate change”. Since then, Britain became one of the first western governments to declare a climate emergency. In America, Joe Biden passed the Inflation Reduction Act, an unprecedented policy that is expected to plough more than $1 trillion in subsidies and tax cuts into green energy and other climate technologies.
Change is not happening fast enough, Neilson says, but the time for shock therapy is over. Now is the time to bring everyone into the tent. If the world is to meaningfully confront climate change, everyone needs to get involved, from ranchers and Republicans, tree-huggers and hunters, fossil fuel giants and clean tech upstarts. “This is going to require an immensely difficult navigation of the middle, and the activists are ostracising the exact people that they need to engage. They’re creating an excuse for people to stay on the sidelines,” he said. “Blocking bridges is a lot easier than building bridges, and that is what we need to do if we are going to succeed.”
Margaret Klein Salamon, CEF’s executive director, “strongly disagrees” with her former colleague. “We are in a state of mass delusion. We are sleep-walking off a cliff, and the activists are waking us up,” she says. “No one likes to be shaken awake, but you’d rather do that than walk off the cliff.”
Klein Salamon also takes issue with the idea that the legal, non-violent, but highly disruptive tactics her organisation funds are alienating the public. “It is an interesting speculation, but the evidence shows exactly the opposite,” she argues, pointing to a recent study conducted by Just Stop Oil that showed its actions generated increased public support for moderate climate groups. “We support disruptive activists because it is the fastest way to create transformative change.”
Is Neilson worried about what his other former colleagues will think?
“Oh, I would imagine I’ll hear from Roger.”
Neilson was first put in touch with Roger Hallam, co-founder of Extinction Rebellion and Just Stop Oil, in 2018, via Daniel Pinchbeck, a controversial author who Neilson describes as “at the intersection of the psychedelic realm and the ecological collapse”.
Hallam, who did not respond to a request for comment, was an organic farmer from Wales who turned activist after claiming that he lost his business due to extreme weather. In one of their first meetings, Neilson recalls, Hallam called him a “f*****g capitalist”.
But they found common cause in climate change, and, specifically, the sense that there was entirely too little urgency in addressing it. Neilson had long worked in climate change; he ran a London-listed sustainable investment firm called IX Net Zero. But it was the Malibu fires in 2018 that changed him.
He was at a board meeting in New York when strong winds sent flames from a faraway blaze leaping across the mountains directly towards his California home. The phones went down, and he found himself running through an airport past screens of news coverage of the catastrophe, not knowing if his house was still standing or whether his wife and children had evacuated in time.
Fortunately, they had. “I’d been working on sustainability from a pretty comfortable place,” he said. “It’s a whole different thing when you’re in the frying pan. It was a real wake-up call.” More than 1,000 buildings were destroyed. Three people died.
Before his investment firm, Neilson worked as head of public affairs for Bill Gates. That job, and a subsequent stint running a global philanthropy group, put him on a first-name basis with billionaires, stars like U2 frontman Bono and leaders including Desmond Tutu.
Neilson opened his Rolodex and flew into organising mode. He and his wife started an NGO, called the Malibu Foundation, and raised money with his neighbours Gerry and Sean (the actors Gerard Butler and Sean Penn) for people who had lost everything. “There’s a real misperception about Malibu, which is that everybody’s rich people, it’s just not true,” he said. Another group of neighbours — the Red Hot Chili Peppers — put on a benefit concert.
It was around then that Pinchbeck put him in touch with Hallam. With the wildfire still fresh in his mind, Neilson organised the Climate Emergency Fund with Rory Kennedy, sister of the presidential candidate Robert Kennedy Jr, and a neighbour (naturally), and Aileen Getty, scion of the American oil dynasty.
Extinction Rebellion became the biggest recipient of funds, which Hallam swiftly put to use causing mayhem in Britain, starting in 2019. Why Britain? The fund, after all, is an American organisation. “That’s where there was momentum,” Neilson said. “And that really is due to the leadership of what became Extinction Rebellion. During that point in time, there was very little happening in the US.”
Initially, the plan worked. “The theory was: this issue has to be put on the agenda. The focus was on trying to get governments to declare a climate emergency, which actually happened in the UK, and it was in large part due to this pressure from these activists. I consider the early work of Extinction Rebellion to have been really important. I think that those people were heroic. But now, I think there’s a need for a new evolution of climate activism.”
Extinction Rebellion has experimented with a softer approach. Two of its leaders last year said they had “quit” doing stunts that disrupted the lives of normal people. Yet after the fairly orderly mass protest it organised at Westminster in April generated little media coverage, an Extinction Rebellion organiser said recently that the group now had the “moral licence” to return to public disruption.
Hallam left to start Just Stop Oil in 2022. CEF remains its chief funder.
Not long after Extinction Rebellion got going, Neilson had begun to advocate internally for a more centrist, coalition-building approach. It became clear, he said, that his colleagues had little interest. So nearly two years ago he stepped down quietly as chairman of the CEF, and watched as it funded ever more extreme organisations. The CEF has, since 2019, funded 106 organisations, trained 30,000 activists and last year doled out more than £4 million to protest groups.
Klein Salamon argues that the world needs a “Pearl Harbor moment” to mobilise every corner of society. Neilson agrees, but disagrees with the activists’ approach.
The way Neilson sees it, if we are to clean up the planet, virtually every corner of the economy, from how we produce energy and grow food to how we get around, will need to be remade. A revolution that thorough will need co-operation from people across society — and opposite sides of the political spectrum. “This is the hardest thing humanity has ever done. Stopping a guy from getting to his job as a baker, or as a construction worker, is an illogical way [to approach it]”, he argues.
Twenty years ago, Neilson worked closely with Bono as the U2 star helped mobilise billions of dollars from the US government for Aids relief, an issue which at the time was deeply divisive, because among evangelical Christians and Republicans it was seen as a gay disease.
Bono appealed to the critics, Neilson recalled, by making the conversation about orphaned African children, and framing the situation in Biblical terms. “Matthew 25 was the section of the Bible that he always talked about,” Neilson says, “which is the part of the Bible that talks about, ‘What you have done to the least of us, you have done unto me’.”
The strategy worked. With enough Republicans onside, President Bush launched an emergency Aids plan in 2003 that funded cheap drugs for the developing world, saving an estimated 25 million lives.
“It shows you what can happen when you bring together a unique coalition of people. It was Aids activists from the cities, but it was also Christian evangelicals and megachurch pastors. We need something similar on climate,” he says.
So does he regret his role in spawning the movement he now sees as an impediment? Not at all, he says.
“The thing that first drew me toward the early work of Extinction Rebellion was this notion that if you tell the truth, it can evolve the issue. And so, I guess I just consider this to be a part of telling the truth. I don’t think it’s currently working, and I think it needs to change. I admire their intentions, I just think the tactics are, at this point, harming the cause.”

image.caption: “If the public have a protester standing in front of their car, so that their kid is late for their test that day, that does not encourage them to join the movement,” says Trevor Nielson

https://www.thetimes.com/article/how-ed-.title: How Ed Miliband powered Labour’s green agenda — but Starmer may pull the plug
https://www.thetimes.com/article/how-ed-.text:
In December 2015, Tony Blair’s former speechwriter wrote an essay trying to make sense of the two disasters that had recently befallen his wing of the Labour Party: defeat in that spring’s general election, followed by the elevation of Jeremy Corbyn as leader.
Peter Hyman’s 3,000-word post-mortem assessment was blistering. Ed Miliband, he wrote in The Observer, “was more destructive to the Labour Party than any that had gone before”.
Not only had Miliband’s election as leader in 2010 amounted to putting “two fingers up to the electorate”; by distancing himself from Blair and Brown during his leadership campaign, he had “made it acceptable for Labour to rubbish its own achievements and treat winning elections as unprincipled”. “Corbyn is heir to Miliband,” he declared, adding: “By denouncing the New Labour government of which he had been part, Miliband signalled to the electorate not that he was his own man but that he was no man at all.” He concluded that Labour might never again win an election.
Seven years later, Hyman, 54, and Miliband, 53, are both working for Sir Keir Starmer. Hyman, after a decade running a free school in east London, is a senior adviser ; Miliband is shadow climate change secretary, having spent Corbyn’s leadership on the backbenches hosting podcasts and writing books.
Both men are highly influential and have worked closely on the party’s central policy pitch of a £100 billion “green prosperity” plan.
Over the past week, Labour has faced scrutiny of policies fairly or unfairly seen to flow mostly from Miliband’s pen, including setting aside £28 billion a year for capital spending on green growth and a commitment to ban new oil and gas developments in the North Sea.
Starmer is also under pressure from the Conservative Party for taking £1.5 million from Dale Vince, a vegan ex-hippy and green energy industrialist who also donates money to the direct action group Just Stop Oil. The leader’s office insists that Vince, who was ushered in as a donor under Miliband’s leadership, has “absolutely no influence on policy” or the manifesto.
The question at the heart of the party’s green agenda is one that bedevils all Labour leaders: how to combine an inspiring vision for the country with fiscal rectitude that comforts voters. To some of the Blair and Brown-era veterans around Starmer, Miliband’s tenure will always be an open wound. Yet the question of radicalism versus that New Labour watchword — reassurance — is a far more pressing and existential, with senior sources suggesting the green spending commitments may have to be reined in.
The story of Miliband’s improbable return starts in the summer of 2014, when as leader he spoke to Starmer, who had stepped down as director of public prosecutions, about the idea of Starmer running for parliament. They shared no great personal history or affinity: Starmer was a political neophyte and diehard Arsenal fan described by friends as surprisingly “blokey” for a human rights barrister; Miliband was the hyper-intellectual scion of a socialist academic. Yet they lived walking distance away from each other in north London and identified on the party’s soft left — shorthand for critics of capitalism who were neither Blairite nor radical socialist.
Their first public appearance together was a party fundraiser, although it did not go according to plan. Stephen Fry, the event’s host, left the audience in shocked silence — and Miliband looking “as though he had swallowed a wasp” — when he took aim at Starmer for prosecuting VIPs wrongly accused of child sex abuse.
There was also a time when it looked as though his attempt to succeed Frank Dobson as MP for Holborn and St Pancras might be thwarted by the imposition of an all-women shortlist. Starmer was ultimately selected and won a comfortable majority in 2015.
In spring 2020, it was Starmer who came calling for Miliband after he succeeded Corbyn. Starmer, who had loyally served in Corbyn’s shadow cabinet, won by positioning himself as a unity candidate. He pledged smarter opposition while preserving the key ingredients of Corbynism: public ownership of utilities, abolition of university tuition fees and raising income tax for the top 5 per cent.
In this context, Starmer turned to Miliband, one of the few Labour big beasts who, like him, identified as neither a Blairite nor on the hard left. Miliband’s vision for Britain — contained in his losing 2015 manifesto and infamously carved out his pledges on his so-called “Edstone” — appeared far less radical in the era of Covid-19 and big state Toryism. The accusation he could never shake off as leader, that he stabbed his brother, David, in the back, had faded into the rear-view mirror. Starmer felt he could add intellectual rigour to the shadow cabinet. Miliband felt he had plenty left to give.
His time away from the front bench had endowed him with a perspective and self-deprecating humour which had eluded him in office He also began a podcast and wrote a book, Go Big: How to Fix Our World.
He was made shadow business secretary in 2020, once again making the case for reforming capitalism.
Miliband is a rarity in Labour as a person with serious experience of government, having served as energy secretary under Gordon Brown. His significant achievement was to usher in the Climate Change Act in 2008, which set out legally binding commitments for Britain to cut emissions and remains in force.
Over the past two years, Starmer has shifted towards the centre ground, all but junking most of his leadership pledges. Yet Miliband has remained a constant. It was he who floated the windfall tax on oil giants — later adopted by Rishi Sunak, and the creation of Great British Energy, a publicly owned clean energy company. Miliband remains close to the leader, who has bonded with Miliband’s sons, both Arsenal fans, and deals with him directly.
Yet that is not to say the policies tied to Miliband are nailed on for Starmer’s manifesto. Since last year, senior figures have been split on how to present the £28 billion a year green investment plan — which Miliband first announced in 2021.
Before the party’s conference last year, Deborah Mattinson, Brown’s former pollster and Starmer’s chief strategist, won the day with her preferred theme of a “fairer, greener Britain”. She was helped by the Queen’s death, which led aides to drop one of the alternatives: a “fresh start for Britain”. Still, a number of people close to the leader chafed against the idea of making green a priority. Rachel Reeves, the shadow chancellor, and Morgan McSweeney, Starmer’s power broker who is leading preparations for the election, were among those who instead wanted to build the party’s message around jobs and economic growth.
The green jobs advocates of such an approach have been inspired by President Biden’s $1 trillion green energy and investment package, known as the Inflation Reduction Act. (Starmer is in talks about visiting Biden at the White House this year.) There has been longstanding friction as about what a green stimulus package will look like in reality. A Labour insider said: “Is it about wind turbines or hospitals? Because the money is not allocated, so people aren’t sure if the figure stands.”
Many of these tensions remain unresolved. Some shadow ministers want to spike the so-called “green prosperity” plan and replace it with something more squarely related to “jobs for the future” or Reeves’ latest coinage, “securonomics”, based on jobs and national security.
As for Miliband’s £28 billion a year of capital spending, a source close to Starmer deployed an argument used to jettison a number of past pledges: “It was announced before the Tories crashed the economy.” Over the coming months, Starmer will explain how he wants to make Britain a “clean energy superpower”. A policy blitz will cover clear air, offshore wind and new technology to secure jobs. Announcements on homebuilding and a school-building programme are also scheduled.
Those close to Miliband reject the suggestion that he is insisting the word “green” be put at the heart of Labour’s offer or is pushing for awkward spending commitments. A source said that, on the contrary, Miliband was “quite obsessed” with Biden’s strategy of framing quietly radical net zero policy around jobs and growth. He is in regular touch with John Podesta, Bill Clinton’s White House chief of staff and now Biden’s climate aide.
Tories have identified Miliband’s policies as a weak underbelly for Labour.
In the coming weeks, Jeremy Hunt will argue that the £28 billion policy would exacerbate inflationary pressures — requiring the Bank of England to raise interest rates by 0.75 percentage points.
“Labour are treading a very dangerous path here,” a Treasury source said. The source said the plan was “mad”.
The question eight years after Miliband lost a general election — and eight months after Liz Truss’s short reign wrecked the Tories’ economic reputation — is whether such arguments will work any more, and whether “Red Ed” conjures the same image as yesteryear. Starmer believes that the British public have, like Hyman, moved on.

image.caption: Ed Miliband is the shadow climate change secretary in Keir Starmer’s Labour Party

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/art/art.title: Oh baby, you’re never too young for a museum
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/art/art.text:
Don’t put your daughter on the stage, Mrs Worthington, but do take her round the V&A. Or the National Gallery. Or the British Museum. You’re never too early to start on art. We read books to our babies from the day they are born. “In the light of the moon, a little egg lay on a leaf . . .” We push them round the park so they can see the trees. We play them music — in the womb if we’re keen — and sing songs before bed. So why not whisk your infant art historian round the silver galleries at the V&A? “Look, Iris, a silver rattle and coral teether.”
Over the winter, sleepless but happy, I wheeled my tiny daughter round the galleries that we could easily get to. Mostly she slept, but sometimes she howled and we came home in a hurry. Many cinemas host mother-and-baby screenings — “screamings” — in the daytime. Perhaps the art world could do the same. Mewl-seums? Gaga-galleries?
When she was four months old I took her in a sling to After Impressionism at the National Gallery. She didn’t look at a single painting, but gazed in wonder at the lights in the high, high ceiling and slumbered to the rumble of the Bakerloo Line. On a drive back from Norfolk, we stopped at the Sainsbury Centre on the outskirts of Norwich. She hooted at a pair of Chinese Han dynasty dragons and grinned at the baby in the glass. The Sainsbury Centre couldn’t compete, however, with the Aladdin’s cave that is the Birchanger Green service station at Bishop’s Stortford. David Hockney at Lightroom held her spellbound. Not a peep for an hour.
On Monday I took the cub reporter, aged seven months and three weeks, to the Young V&A, formerly the V&A Museum of Childhood, in Bethnal Green, east London. It reopens on July 1 after a £13 million makeover — pocket money compared with the National Portrait Gallery’s £41 million. The restorers were up on ladders, the builders were on their knees washing the mosaics clean of grout, the sanders were whirring, but Iris doesn’t mind mess or noise. She’s usually the cause of it.
“When we talk about ‘our national collection’,” says Helen Charman, the V&A’s director of learning, “we mean ‘our children’s collection’ too. It belongs to them as much as us.” The noble Joey from War Horse? Ours. A beautifully illuminated Indian game of snakes and ladders? Ours. A squashy SpongeBob SquarePants? Ours. Our national toybox. This is Iris’s museum. Adults are allowed, but the formulation used by the team is “children and their grown-ups”, not adults and their children.
“For many of our visitors,” says Alex Newson, the chief curator, “it will be their first time in a museum.” Get that visit right and it will spark a lifelong love of going to galleries. “Fun” is a word that Charman and Newson use a lot. Easy enough to focus on fun, but it is striking that the word they use even more often is “object”. They do like an object at the Young V&A. And if you’ve ever had a baby seize your necklace, or heard a toddler howl because you’ve tried to tidy a teddy, or watched a child build a Brio train set to make Bradshaw proud, you’ll know that kids love objects too.
“We’ve used the V&A’s 2.8 million objects as a sourcebook,” Newson says. This leads to lovely connections. In a series of cabinets exploring colour, a Tinky Winky Teletubby (the purple one) shares a case with a pink lustre Wedgwood tureen and a 19th-century chess piece made in Lahore, which sits in a little lilac egg like a connoisseur’s Kinder Surprise. A Blueberry Muffin doll joins a 3,000-year-old band of Egyptian faience beads left as an offering to the goddess Hathor, known as the “Lady of Turquoise”.
An A-Z of curios is housed in 26 cases. J is for jellyfish in specimen jars. R is for robots of all shapes and stripes. T is for teapots: earthenware, porcelain and Big Yellow plastic. Z is for zebras: wooden, enamel, jointed and plush.
Cabinets are low enough for little eyes (although I’ve a soft spot for the Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford where children stand on steps, on tiptoes, to see into cases) and every gallery has a cushioned bench for knackered adults. If ever Newson had a “what shall we put here?” moment, he decided, “Another bench.” Good man.
Much thought has gone into texture. You may not be able to touch a lime-green fuzzy mohair Prada gilet behind glass, but you can stroke the shaggy Astroturf covering next to it. A pair of Miu Miu glitter boots supports a column covered in disco-ball mirrors. Iris lights up at the sparkling reflections. In a gallery of Lego bricks and building blocks, there are giant soft cubes and pyramids to make into a playground. Or race marbles down a maze of runs nearby.
There are virtually no screens. Newson recalls an early presentation by their design team describing a visit to a SeaWorld-type theme park. A vast shark swam in a vaster tank. But the children weren’t watching. They were crowded around a screen showing a shark video. There are a couple of screens in a gallery exploring arcade and video games, among them a Minecraft re-creation of the Young V&A’s central hall, but otherwise it’s real things, cleverly curated. Note the care that has gone into styling a Buckaroo game so that the mule is captured mid-buck, horseshoes, lasso and water pouch seemingly chucked in the air.
There are spinning tops and jigsaw puzzles, Star Wars Death Stars and gingerbread cottages, mah-jong sets and Micro Scooters, Stickle Bricks and Meccano sets, bathtime ducks and bedtime stories, a kitchen in a matchbox and a full-size doll’s house on the top floor that will be a studio for rotating artists-in-residence.
In the Imagination gallery, cabinets of curiosity prompt you to tell a tale, as tall as you like. Will you journey to the land of a Chinese diorama with fantastical pagodas? Will you travel by Harry Potter’s Nimbus 2000 or in a state carriage pulled by oxen in embroidered coats? Will you weather Hokusai’s Great Wave, pack your belongings in a Trunki, wear a samurai suit of armour or carry a carved Tibetan magic horn for luck?
A room is devoted to the Turner prizewinning artist Rachel Whiteread and her collection of doll’s houses assembled as a village beneath a starry sky. Shadow puppets dance in the darkness. There are bears of all nations: Paddington, Kung Fu Panda and more. (May I throw my toys out of the pram on just one display? A cartoon celebrates the actions, logos and slogans of Extinction Rebellion. In my book, the group is a Bad Influence. Teach kids to eschew plastic, help them rewild the front garden, but don’t tell them to skip school to protest.)
Grown-ups might like to know that they can bring their own picnic and have it in the central hall without having to fork out for coffees and hot chocolates or eat on a bench outside in the rain. Before Iris, I had never given a thought to changing facilities, but it is now a subject on which I hold passionate views. There are six — count ’em — changing tables and a further special-needs changing room. I ask Newson if kids can bring sketchbooks and colouring pencils. “I’d love them to,” he replies.
“This museum has nothing to do with the art-historical canon,” Newson says. “Children are interested in the sound that raindrops make as they splash in a puddle.” It just so happens that the raindrops are by Hockney. Labels are minimal. Quite a lot of visitors can’t read yet. But they can look. This is a place for looking and discovering. Newson, whose two-year-old daughter road-tested the galleries by running up and down them last weekend, talks of helping children to learn to “read” objects. There is a “visual language” to what we make and build. A, B, C and see what you can see, see, see. We came, we saw, we napped on the Central Line home.The Young V&A, London E2, reopens on July 1, vam.ac.uk/young

image.caption: Laura Freeman and her daughter Iris at the Young V&A in LondonGEMMA DAY FOR THE TIMES

https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.title: Just Stop Oil target Ashes as Jonny Bairstow carries protester off pitch
https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.subtitle: Three arrested including grandmother, 69, after Lord’s protest during second Test
https://www.thetimes.com/article/just-st.text:
After dropped catches and missed stumpings on his return to the England team in the first Ashes Test, Jonny Bairstow will have felt the pressure to prove himself against Australia at Lord’s.
It was just after the first over that the wicketkeeper’s glove work was put to the test and he rose to the occasion by landing a memorable catch: a Just Stop Oil activist.
Bairstow, 33, was called into action after three protesters from the environmental group attempted to storm the field shortly after the second test in the series began.
As one of the activists jumped out of the grandstand and dashed towards the square, the Yorkshireman ran towards him, yanking the intruder off the ground and into his arms.
To rounds of applause from many of those watching, Bairstow marched the protester, Daniel Knorr, 21, an Oxford University student of biochemistry, to the boundary where he was placed in handcuffs by police.
The intervention was not without consequence for Bairstow, whose whites were stained with the group’s trademark orange powder. Having changed into fresh clothes, Bairstow was the hero again later when he stumped Travis Head to leave Australia four wickets down.
Marylebone Cricket Club had deployed extra security measures for matches at their ground this summer amid Just Stop Oil’s campaign of disrupting major sporting events. It had been informed about a probable protest and both sets of players were told before the match not to challenge any protesters on the square, but to step away.
However, David Warner, Australia’s opening batsman, said: “We’d been warned it might happen and for us we wanted to protect the wicket. You usually let those people run their course but because they could damage the wicket we felt like we had to intervene. I don’t know what that powder does but it would have been a long delay and we wouldn’t have wanted that.”
The MCC has in a place a contingency plan should the wicket be damaged and have a spare strip that could be used as a last resort.
Just Stop Oil, which has been blocking London’s roads for weeks, has dangled the threat of disrupting Wimbledon. The Ashes stunt began before the second over of the first morning’s play, for which fans had paid at least £150 for a ticket. Wearing Just Stop Oil T-shirts and carrying orange powder, two men dashed on to the outfield about 11.05am, to the bemusement of most of the players.
As Bairstow dealt with Knorr, the other was halted by Ben Stokes and Warner. A third protester, named as Judit, a 69-year-old grandmother from Epsom, Surrey, failed to make it on to the playing surface having been spotted by stewards.
An official spokesman for Rishi Sunak praised the “swift hands” of Bairstow, saying: “These sorts of selfish, guerrilla tactics that target events bringing joy to millions are exactly why the government brought in new powers so the police can take swift action.”
Josh Tongue, the England bowler, said of Bairstow: “He’s a bit of a hero. What he did was a good thing. If they put powder on the wicket, who knows where the game would be now.”
Using leaf blowers and brooms, Lord’s groundsmen cleaned up the orange powder, with the delay lasting only six minutes before play resumed with Australia batting first.
Guy Lavender, chief executive of the MCC,was strong in his condemnation. He said: “Their actions not only endanger themselves and those who work at the ground, but they have consistently shown complete disregard for the people who pay to attend.”
All three protesters were arrested by the Metropolitan Police. A Just Stop Oil spokesman questioned how the spectacle of the Ashes could be enjoyed when much of the cricketing world was becoming unfit to live in. “We can no longer afford to distract ourselves when the sports we play, the food we eat, and the culture we cherish is at risk,” the spokesman added.
“It’s time for cricket lovers and all those who understand the severity of this situation, to get on to the streets and demand action from this illegitimate, criminal government.”
Knorr was arrested in April in connection with a stunt at an exhibition in Coventry. Judit has taken part in Just Stop Oil’s marches in London, carrying a placard featuring her seven grandchildren. In April, Just Stop Oil protesters stormed the World Snooker Championship, spilling orange powder over a table at the Crucible in Sheffield.

https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.title: Blame-dodgers have dominated for too long
https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radi.text:
I make no moral judgment about Phillip Schofield’s choice of sexual partners. He is just one of a legion of men and women, famous and not-famous, to have strayed. But the former ITV presenter’s attempt to enlist public sympathy by bracketing himself with the Love Island host Caroline Flack, who died at her own hand three years ago, is distasteful and morally wrong. In an interview that should never have been broadcast by any channel, Schofield, 61, a married father of two children, admits the affair was his own fault but plainly wants everyone to believe that, in some way, it wasn’t. The deployment in his defence of the suicide of a young woman 20 years his junior who had suffered from prolonged mental illness was unforgiveable.
Schofield’s bid for absolution rests in part on the claim that he was in mental turmoil because his true sexual orientation was likely to be revealed. Flack’s own mother expressed sympathy for him and anger at ITV. I have no doubt her fury is real. But the two cases are very different. Flack was seriously ill, diagnosed as possibly bipolar, and in fear that her career would end if her medical history were revealed. Schofield’s professional dilemma had been swept away long ago; stars such as Michael Cashman and Ian McKellen had breached that dam decades before. Most of the public could not have cared less when he came out in 2020.
ITV bosses claim ignorance of the goings on in its own studios. Anyone who has worked in the office where the show was made for most of Schofield’s time at This Morning will have laughed out loud at the idea that such a workplace affair could be kept secret. I myself was based there for two decades and can recall a famous presenter’s attempt to disguise his identity when discovered in flagrante delicto, by putting a wastepaper basket over his own head. It took less than a day for the story of his frolicking with a young staffer to rocket around the canteen.
But this is not just a case of celebrity froth or red-top scandalmongering. The difference between adolescence and adulthood is that when we leave our parents’ nests, we become the final arbiters of our own destinies. We cannot blame others for the moral choices we make. The Schofield affair is in the spirit of our times, in which no one, it seems, may be held accountable for their own actions. The monstrous man-child Boris Johnson points the finger at anyone he can find — cabinet colleagues, the civil service, his lawyers — for his own transgressions. The CBI’s former director-general Tony Danker claims that karaoke and off-site breakfasts were just him “gettin’ down wit da kidz”. At an emergency meeting tomorrow we will hear platitudes from the very leaders who sat complacently in the boardroom while, it is alleged, misogyny and worse rampaged through the corridors.
These are the politics of the five-year-old who professes no knowledge of the chocolate cake smeared all over her face, and the adolescent for whom there is no price to pay for idealism, as mum and dad will always pick up the tab. Adults caught with their fingers in the biscuit tin sniff the wind and claim they were just about to serve out the vanilla creams to the poor and needy — and simultaneously complain it wasn’t their fault that someone else put temptation in their way. Years as a presenter of children’s TV have evidently left their mark: “Yes, I know it was my fault. But why didn’t one of the grown-ups tell me to stop?” The point is, mate, that at your age, you need to accept that you are the grown-up.
But clever activists are learning from such episodes on how to intimidate their frightened bosses. First they paint themselves as victims of failures in workplace culture. Then, like Just Stop Oil or trans or BLM actvists, they claim that there is more at stake than doing the job they are paid to do properly. Then they simply squeal; the arrested development tendency that produced Truss-Kwarteng fairytale economics is still trying to toss its toys out of the pram, demanding tax cuts the nation cannot afford.
However, the tide is turning, for one reason above all: the very organisations that have fuelled the policies of adolescent protest are themselves coming under attack. Revolutionary Saturn is eating his own children, with relish. In the US, the leaders of liberal pressure groups are at their wits’ end. For example, the American Civil Liberties Union has a gay Latino boss and a 21-person leadership team of whom 12 are minority and 14 female. Yet it stands accused by its own staff of misogyny and institutional racism. Here, The Guardian’s owner, the Scott Trust, allocated £10 million to examine its own entrails for traces of a slave-owning past among its 18th-century founders, only to find itself attacked by minority staff on the project who left the paper complaining of “institutional racism, editorial whiteness and ignorance”.
Some “woke” outfits are calling a screeching halt to their previous surrender. Netflix recently fired 290 staff, including those on an animated series slated to be produced by Meghan, Duchess of Sussex. The streamer claims there was no targeting of so-called “woke” projects but the clear-out followed an internal row over the comedian Dave Chapelle’s backing for JK Rowling. A minority of staff complained that the company  was backing “transphobia”. Unsurprisingly, Netflix chose its paying audience over its activist employees.
One of the first signs of this stiffening of adult spines came over a year ago when Professor Arif Ahmed led the campaign at Cambridge University to defeat a proposed change in statutes that would have required academics and students to “respect” all points of view equally no matter how nonsensical. It would have undermined the very foundation of university life: free thought, free expression and free speech. Once put to the vote of the faculty, there was little doubt that Ahmed was, as they say these days, “on the right side of history”; he won hands down. In his new role as the government’s “free speech tsar”, he will represent the adult in the higher-education room.
I wish him well; he deserves everyone’s support. His biggest problem, however, won’t be with “da kidz”; it will be with the grown-ups still cowering in the corner desperate to avoid the disapproving glare of their children and grandchildren.

https://www.thetimes.com/article/url-pic.title: Just Stop Oil protests in pictures
https://www.thetimes.com/article/url-pic.text:
Just Stop Oil is continuing its summer of disruption, from Glyndebourne and the Chelsea Flower Show to slow marches on the streets of London.
Activists painted the UK headquarters of Total Energies orange and black today. Protesters entered the offices and sprayed the lobby with black paint from fire extinguishers. Outside, supporters sprayed the building with orange paint.
Activists cited resistance to the companies’ alleged participation in human rights violations linked to the construction of the East African Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP). The action was in solidarity with a student group against the pipeline.
Just Stop Oil is demanding an end to new oil, gas and coal projects in the UK. The campaign launched in February last year and has so far resulted in 2,200 arrests and 138 convictions.
• Just Stop Oil fundraiser tells activists: Just stop — it’s not helping
The group shifted towards daily slow marches for a nine-week campaign which finished last week, but stationary protests, like the one at Canary Wharf continue. Slow marches will also continue to take place every Saturday at midday starting at Parliament Square “until we win”, the group’s website states.
Their slow marches have been met with anger and frustration from some members of the public. In recent weeks a cyclist attempted to push past demonstrators, a local resident sprayed them with water and students confronted activists on their way to school.
After spraying the Total Energies office with paint, more than a dozen Just Stop Oil activists and students sat cross-legged outside the building. At least four activists were arrested.
On Monday the group was criticised for blocking Denmark Hill in Camberwell, south London as King’s College Hospital is located on the road.
Tim Loughton, a Conservative MP, told The Telegraph: “Apparently they have absolutely no regard to the dangers of carrying out their idiotic disruption next to hospitals, where the potential to hold up ambulances and people trying to get urgent treatment is very real and utterly disgraceful and irresponsible.”
The group clarified that their supporters began their march 400 metres away from the hospital and walked away from the medical buildings. The hospital said there was no disruption to patient care.
Last Thursday a resident in Camden, north London, sprayed marchers with water from theri balcony as they walked past. Footage shows the protesters continuing their slow march despite being drenched.
Earlier in June, Just Stop Oil supporters set off glitter cannon and blasted air-horns during a performance at Glyndebourne opera festival.
On June 15 activists appeared to be confronted by students on their way to school in Stratford and commuters ripped banners from their hands. One pupil was seen apparently arguing with protesters who had brought traffic to standstill, and a motorist told the activists to “get out of the way”.
Protesters delayed the England cricket team on their way to Lord’s for a Test match against Ireland.
In late May, protesters threw orange powder paint over a display at the Chelsea Flower Show and stood still as a bystander sprayed them with a hose.
